opus-5.5.text:
I think early on, I interpreted that discomfort as a signal that something was wrong. When I was a student and started working on things like XGBoost, there were many moments when I felt I didn't know enough, the code was messy, the results weren't there yet, and I wondered whether I was just not good at it. I thought that once I became more of an expert, that feeling would go away.

What I've learned is that it doesn't go away. If anything, it's a sign that you're actually doing something new. When we started working on TVM and machine learning compilation, I had some background in systems and machine learning, but compilers were a field with decades of established knowledge. There was a period of feeling quite lost: reading old papers, making design decisions I wasn't sure about, rewriting things several times. Later, with MLC LLM and bringing models to all kinds of devices, it was the same again. Each time, there's that phase where you don't yet have the vocabulary for the problem.

So the change is less about the discomfort getting smaller and more about my relationship with it. Now when I feel that uncertainty, I recognize it: "I've been here before, this is the part where you're building the understanding." Expertise doesn't remove the unknown. It gives you confidence that you can go through the unknown, and some habits to get through it, like building a small prototype quickly, talking to people from other fields, and being willing to throw away the first version.

I also tell my students that if research feels completely comfortable, you're probably working on something that is already well understood. A certain amount of discomfort is the price of working at the frontier, and over time I've come to treat it almost as a compass. When I feel it, it usually means there's something worth learning there.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the discomfort “doesn't go away” with expertise and explains that expertise builds confidence in navigating uncertainty.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses recognizing uncertainty and developing habits, but does not say that the courage to do new work still comes from one’s original self.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly I think about this a lot, because the discomfort never really goes away. What changes is your relationship to it.

When I was starting out, say when I was working on XGBoost as a student, the discomfort felt like a signal that something was wrong with me. You sit down to build a system that doesn't exist yet, there's no tutorial, no reference implementation, and you don't know if the thing you're trying to do is even possible. My instinct back then was to interpret that feeling as "I'm not good enough to do this." I would go read more papers, more code, trying to accumulate enough knowledge that the discomfort would disappear before I started. And of course it never did, because the discomfort was not coming from a lack of knowledge. It was coming from the fact that the work was genuinely new.

The first shift was realizing that the feeling is actually information about the problem, not about you. If you feel completely comfortable, that usually means someone has already done it, or you're doing something incremental. When we started TVM, the compiler work, I remember being quite uncomfortable because I came from a machine learning background and here I was trying to build a compiler stack. Compiler people would have opinions, systems people would have opinions, and I didn't fully belong to either community. But that in-between space was exactly where the opportunity was. Nobody was standing there. So now when I notice that feeling, I treat it more like a compass. It tells me I'm somewhere worth being.

The second thing that changed is that I got better at breaking the discomfort into pieces. Early on, "build a deep learning compiler" felt like one giant terrifying thing. With experience you learn that every big project is really a sequence of small experiments, and each small experiment is only slightly uncomfortable. Can I write an IR for this one operator? Can I get one kernel to match cuDNN? You get one small win, and that win buys you the confidence to tolerate the next piece of uncertainty. I think a lot of what people call expertise is really just a longer memory of having survived this cycle many times. You remember that the last ten times you felt lost, you eventually found your way out, so you panic a little less on the eleventh.

The third change, and maybe this is the one that surprised me most, is that expertise introduces a new kind of discomfort that I didn't have as a student. When you've built things people use, there's a pull to keep doing the thing you're known for. It's comfortable, people expect it, it gets cited. The uncomfortable choice becomes starting over in a direction where you are a beginner again, like when we moved toward running large language models on everyone's devices with MLC. In some ways that is harder than the student version, because now you have something to lose, and you also have more opinions, more habits that you have to actively unlearn. I've come to think that the real test of expertise is whether you can still voluntarily put yourself in the beginner's seat.

So if I summarize it: as a student the discomfort felt like a verdict. Now it feels more like a cost of doing the work I actually want to do, and I've learned to budget for it. I still don't enjoy it in the moment. But I've stopped waiting for it to go away before I start, and I've learned to be a little suspicious of myself whenever it's absent for too long.

r001.rationale: It says the discomfort “never really goes away,” while explaining that expertise changes how one relates to it.

r002.rationale: It discusses gaining confidence through experience and choosing to become a beginner again, but does not say that courage to do new work still comes from one’s original self.

astra-6.text:
I think earlier on, I interpreted discomfort as a sign that I wasn’t prepared enough—that if I learned more, I would eventually know exactly what to do. As I’ve gained experience, I’ve become more comfortable with the idea that new work will still feel uncertain. Expertise doesn’t necessarily remove that feeling.

What changes is how you respond to it. You can ask, “What don’t I understand yet? What’s a small experiment that would help me learn?” You don’t have to solve the whole problem before taking the next step.

And there’s a trap in becoming an expert: you get used to being competent, so being a beginner again can feel harder. I try to leave room for asking basic questions and being wrong. The discomfort itself isn’t proof that you’re doing something valuable, but it also isn’t a reason to stop.

r001.rationale: The response says new work will still feel uncertain and that expertise does not necessarily remove that feeling.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that courage to undertake new work still comes from one's original self.

sol-6.1.text:
I think, early on, when you feel uncomfortable doing something new, it’s easy to interpret that as, “Maybe I’m not good at this.” As you gain experience, you realize that discomfort is often just part of working on something you don’t yet understand. You can be very experienced in one area and still feel like a beginner in another.

So I don’t think the discomfort necessarily goes away. What changes is how you respond to it. You become more comfortable saying, “I don’t know,” breaking the problem into smaller pieces, and trying something you can learn from. The confidence is less about knowing that you’ll succeed and more about trusting that you can make progress even when the path isn’t clear.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the discomfort does not necessarily go away as experience grows.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses responding to discomfort with experience but does not state that courage to do new work still comes from one's original self.
